Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . sampled: Homarus gammarus, also known as the European or common lobster, is a clawed lobster species inhabiting the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and parts of the Black Sea. Closely related to the American lobster (H. americanus), this species can grow up to 60 cm (24 in) long and weigh as much as 6 kilograms (13 lb), easily identified by its large claws. Live lobsters are blue in color, only turning the characteristic "lobster red" upon cooking. Mating occurs in summer, with females carrying eggs for up to a year until they hatch into planktonic larvae. Highly valued as a food item, Homarus gammarus is frequently caught using lobster pots, especially around the British Isles.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is a large crustacean that can grow up to 60 cm (24 in) in length and weigh 5–6 kg (11–13 lb). However, lobsters caught in traps are usually between 23–38 cm (9–15 in) long and weigh 0.7–2.2 kg (1.5–4.9 lb). Like other crustaceans, lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed to grow, a process called ecdysis or moulting. Younger lobsters may moult several times a year, while larger lobsters only moult every 1–2 years.

The first pair of walking legs is characterized by distinct, dissimilar claws. The larger claw, the "crusher," has rounded teeth-like structures specifically for crushing food items. In contrast, the "cutter" claw has sharp inner margins used for gripping or tearing apart food. Usually, the left claw acts as the crusher, and the right claw functions as the cutter.

A lobster's shell is usually blue with mottled spots on top and yellow underneath. The characteristic red color we associate with lobsters appears only after cooking. This happens because the red pigment, astaxanthin, is typically hidden by a protein bond. When heat is applied during cooking, this bond breaks down, releasing the astaxanthin and making the lobster turn red.

*Homarus gammarus* exhibits the closest evolutionary relationship to the American lobster, *Homarus americanus*. The two species display considerable commonalities and are able to interbreed under controlled laboratory conditions. Nevertheless, natural crossbreeding is unlikely because their natural distributions do not overlap. Several distinguishing features exist between them.

European female lobsters (Homarus gammarus) reach sexual maturity when their carapace measures 80–85 mm (3.1–3.3 in), slightly longer than the size at which males mature. Mating typically occurs during the summer, between a male with a hard shell and a female who has recently molted and has a soft shell. The female then carries the eggs, attached to her abdominal appendages, for up to a year, depending on the water temperature. These egg-bearing females, referred to as "berried," can be seen throughout the year.

The eggs hatch during the night, and the emerging larvae swim up to the surface. They then float along with the currents, preying on zooplankton. This larval stage, which involves three molts, spans roughly 15 to 35 days. After the third molt, the young crabs start to resemble adults and move to the ocean floor. These juvenile crabs are seldom seen in the wild and, as a result, are poorly understood, although we know they build complex burrows. It is believed that only a very small number of larvae, approximately 1 out of 20,000, make it to the seafloor stage. Once the young crabs reach a shell length of 15 mm (0.59 in), they leave their burrows and start their adult lives.

Homarus gammarus, the European lobster, lives in the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, from northern Norway down to the Azores and Morocco, although it is not found in the Baltic Sea. Its range covers a large portion of the Mediterranean Sea, stopping before the area east of Crete, and it appears only on the northwestern coast of the Black Sea. Its northern boundary includes the Norwegian fjords, which lie inside the Arctic Circle.

This species is composed of four distinct genetic groups: a prevalent, widespread population and three others that have undergone independent evolution, probably as a result of limited population size and adjustment to particular local environments. Among these is the lobster population of northern Norway, recognized as the "midnight sun lobster." Additionally, lobster populations in the Mediterranean Sea exhibit genetic differences compared to those in the Atlantic Ocean. The last separate group resides in the Netherlands, where samples from an unspecified location differed from those obtained in the North Sea or English Channel.

A project aimed to introduce the European lobster, H. gammarus, to New Zealand, mirroring attempts to introduce other European species such as the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. Between 1904 and 1914, a million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin, but the species did not successfully establish itself.

*Homarus gammarus*, the European lobster, typically resides on the continental shelf from the surface down to 150 meters (492 feet), with the majority inhabiting shallower waters less than 50 meters (160 feet) deep. They prefer solid substrates such as rocky or hardened muddy seabeds, utilizing natural crevices or burrows for protection and emerging at night to search for sustenance.

The European lobster, *Homarus gammarus*, is susceptible to gaffkaemia, a disease caused by the bacterium *Pediococcus homari*. Although prevalent in American lobsters, this disease has only been found in captive *H. gammarus*, and in those instances, it was impossible to rule out prior contamination of the tanks by American lobsters (*H. americanus*).

The European lobster, or Homarus gammarus, is a highly prized food item, with evidence of its culinary appeal dating back to a 17th-century English folk song. Sold fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered, it fetches top prices. Its succulent white meat is found in the claws and abdomen, and nearly the entire cephalothorax is edible, excluding the "sand vein" (gut) and gastric mill. Due to its reputation for superior flavor, H. gammarus can be significantly more expensive, costing up to three times as much as the American lobster, H. americanus.

Lobster pots are the main method for catching lobsters, although baited lines using octopus or cuttlefish can sometimes draw them out, allowing them to be caught by net or by hand. In 2008, the total catch of *H. gammarus* in Europe and North Africa reached 4,386 tonnes, with the British Isles (including the Channel Islands) contributing 3,462 tonnes (79%) of that amount. The smallest permissible size for landing *H. gammarus* is a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 in).

*Homarus gammarus* is the official type species for the genus *Homarus* Weber, 1795, a designation established by Direction 51 of the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Prior to this, the species was referred to by different names like *Astacus marinus* Fabricius, 1775, and *Homarus vulgaris* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837, which led to ambiguity. This was exacerbated because Friedrich Weber's initial genus description went unnoticed until Mary Rathbun's rediscovery, thereby nullifying any prior type species designations (for *Homarus* H. Milne-Edwards, 1837) for *Homarus* Weber, 1795.

In 1974, Holthuis identified a specific specimen as the lectotype for the European lobster, Homarus gammarus. This lobster was collected from the sea near Marstrand, Sweden, located at 57°53′ N 11°32′ E, approximately 48 km (30 miles) northwest of Gothenburg. Regrettably, the lectotype itself and precise information about its collection site are now missing.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam (1914–1976) was a distinguished Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) officer. Born and educated in Tasmania, he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Before World War II, he specialized in flight instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, which operated Lockheed Hudsons. Deployed to Dutch Timor in December, the squadron fought against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. Headlam returned to Australia in February 1942, holding several staff and training roles, and reached the rank of group captain by the war's end.

Headlam's career progressed after World War II, beginning with his command of the North-Western Area in 1946 and his tenure as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. He served as commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing and later at RAF Tengah in Singapore during the Malayan Emergency of 1950–51. He twice acted as Air Member for Personnel, in 1957 and again from 1959 to 1960, and was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. Promoted to air vice marshal, he then held positions as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command (1961–62), AOC No. 224 Group RAF (1962–1965) during the Indonesia–Malaysia confrontation, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (1965–66), and AOC Support Command (1966–67). He was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. Following his role as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam, born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, was the son of farming parents, Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He finished his secondary education at <unk> College in Hobart in 1932. Against his parents' wishes, Headlam joined the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. Following this, he underwent training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and earned his commission as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

After completing his conversion training, Headlam was assigned to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. This squadron, considered the size of a flight according to the official RAAF history before the war, was part of No. 1 FTS and operated aircraft like Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes. While serving here, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and wrote a paper on national defense, arguing that Australia could achieve near invulnerability with "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens contends that this paper essentially "defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept" that has consistently characterized RAAF strategic thought.

Upon completing his flying instructors course in July 1936, Headlam joined the staff at No. 1 FTS and was elevated to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. In July 1938, he was one of six individuals chosen for the RAAF's first Long Specialist Navigation Course at Point Cook, under the guidance of Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch. The course was marked by well-publicized training flights, including a 12-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700 mi) circumnavigation of Australia in November by three Avro Ansons, with Headlam piloting one. The following month, in December, Headlam led the same three Ansons on a six-day journey across Central Australia. He ultimately finished the navigation course with distinction. On January 27, 1939, he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander, first with No. 2 Squadron and subsequently with No. 1 Squadron from August 29, both of which operated Ansons.

At the start of World War II, No. 1 Squadron carried out convoy protection and sea patrols off Australia's southeast coast. Headlam stayed with the squadron as a flight commander until January 15, 1940, when he was reassigned to Headquarters Laverton as the navigation officer for the base. On March 27, he was posted to RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was promoted to squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Two weeks later, he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and they subsequently had a son and a daughter.

In April 1941, Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander in July. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, mainly conducted maritime patrols in the south until December 5. Due to rising concerns about potential Japanese aggression in the Pacific, four of their aircraft were sent to Darwin, Northern Territory. On December 7, this group began operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron remained on alert in Darwin. The following day, with Australia now at war in the Pacific, a Hudson from Penfui attacked the Japanese Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship, forcing it aground. By December 12, Headlam had moved to Penfui, becoming the commanding officer of both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's aircraft were stationed at Penfui and Darwin. The Penfui detachment focused on striking Japanese ships participating in the Celebes invasion. On January 11th, two Hudsons attacked Japanese floatplanes while bombing a transport, reporting three enemy aircraft either destroyed or damaged. However, on January 12th, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. Penfui was first bombed by the Japanese on January 26th, 1942, becoming a regular target, which led to damage to some planes. While the serviceable Hudsons withdrew to Darwin, Headlam and his personnel remained at Penfui to assist reconnaissance missions from Australia. On February 18th, Headlam was instructed to evacuate everyone except a small demolition team, who would collaborate with Sparrow Force to destroy the airfield. He returned to Darwin the following day, on the same day as the city's first Japanese air raid. Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were destroyed in the attack, causing the remaining planes to move to Daly Waters, from where they continued reconnaissance and bombing raids on Japanese forces in Timor.

Headlam remained in Darwin as Controller of Operations at North-Western Area Command Headquarters until May 12, 1942. Subsequently, he was posted to Nhill, Victoria, to take charge of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which employed Ansons. In June, the school's personnel were used to form No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron. On July 20, 1943, Headlam took command of No. 2 Air Observer School in Mount Gambier, South Australia, which also operated Ansons. He was promoted to group captain on December 1, 1943, and eight days later, he became the inaugural commanding officer of No. 3, flying Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. After leaving No. 3, he commenced studies at the RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. He was then appointed senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam became Officer Commanding North-Western Area. By the end of that year, he was in Britain, attending the Royal Air Force Staff College, Andover, and collaborating with RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Returning to Australia in November 1947, he was made Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, Headlam succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, which was based at RAF Changi, Singapore. This Wing controlled RAAF units participating in the Malayan Emergency: No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, flying Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, using Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns executed both broad bombing campaigns in communist zones and precise, targeted attacks. The Dakotas handled courier services, VIP transportation, medical evacuations across South East Asia, and in Malaya, they transported troops and supplies, delivered resources to allied forces, and disseminated propaganda. On December 20, Headlam suffered minor injuries when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he was co-piloting made a crash landing at Kampong Aur in Pahang, caused by engine failure during a supply drop. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, while remaining commander of No. 90 Wing. Headlam gave up his command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

Headlam's career progressed on February 19, 1952, when he became the senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, NSW. As SASO, he oversaw the RAAF's modernization with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. A major reorganization also took place, transitioning the Air Force from a geographic to a functional command system, establishing Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Eastern Area Command, primarily an operational hub due to its numerous combat units, was subsequently transformed into Home Command in October 1953. Headlam's service was honored with an OBE in the 1954 New Year Honours, cited for his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty." He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and his appointment as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on October 7, 1954.

Headlam reached the permanent rank of air commodore on January 1, 1955. The following November, he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and in 1956, he attended the Imperial Defence College. After returning to Australia, he twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra: from March 19 to October 21, 1957, taking over from Air Vice Marshal Fred Scherger and handing over to Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, succeeding Walters and being succeeded by Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. As Air Member for Personnel, Headlam sat on the Air Board, the RAAF's governing body made up of senior officers and headed by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also represented the RAAF on a committee led by William John Allison that examined defence service conditions and suggested improvements, including doubling flight pay. At the Department of Air, Headlam also held the positions of Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, a position with oversight of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the Queen's Birthday Honours of 1958, announced on June 3. In May 1960, he was appointed acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam joined Operational Command (OPCOM), the reorganized entity that took over from Home Command in controlling RAAF operational units. He rose to Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM in April, replacing Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock, and was subsequently promoted to air vice marshal on May 29. Headlam was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya on July 17, 1962, and a week later, became AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore, while Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch succeeded him at OPCOM. As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam directed air defense and offensive operations in the area during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which began officially the following January. Following his divorce in 1956, Headlam married Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, on January 20, 1964, in Sydney. He relinquished his command at No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Headlam's return to Australia saw him appointed Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on January 26, 1965. He was awarded Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on June 22 for his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His tenure as DCAS coincided with the Air Force's largest re-equipment program since World War II, complicated by manpower shortages due to this expansion and Australia's increasing role in Southeast Asian security. Towards the end of his appointment, the first RAAF helicopters were sent to the Vietnam War, leading to a planning visit to Saigon with Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, Chief of the General Staff, in March 1966. A year prior, Wilton's proposal to Chief of the Air Staff, Air Marshal Murdoch, to send two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for training was turned down, leading to the RAAF helicopter squadron's insufficient preparedness for army support tasks upon deployment. On August 8, 1966, Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC Support Command in Melbourne. Support Command, created in 1959, was formed by combining the RAAF's former Training and Maintenance Commands. On January 1, 1968, Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. Additionally, he served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from November 17, 1970, to June 5, 1971.

Headlam returned to Australia in June 1971 and utilized his resettlement leave before formally retiring from the Air Force on August 3rd. He made his home in Melbourne, where he died at 62 years old on December 23, 1976, after a lengthy battle with cancer. His children and second wife outlived him, and his funeral was a private affair, succeeded by cremation at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state highway in Michigan's Lower Peninsula that links Fremont and Howard City. The portion of the route between Newaygo and Howard City goes through Fremont and runs along the southern edge of Manistee National Forest. The M-82 designation has been used before in Michigan, appearing in the Upper Peninsula as early as 1919. The existing Lower Peninsula route was established in the 1920s. Its western end has been modified over the years, previously extending to New Era and Hesperia, before the current route configuration was finalized in the late 1970s.

M-82 begins at the tri-county point west of Fremont, where it meets M-120 and B-96. At this junction, M-120 serves as the north-south boundary between Newaygo and both Oceana and Muskegon counties, while B-96 runs west, forming the Oceana-Muskegon county line. From here, M-82 proceeds east along 48th Street through rural farmland toward Fremont, becoming Main Street as it bisects the city. Leaving Fremont, M-82 turns south onto Stewart Avenue before curving east onto 72nd Street, continuing through agricultural areas. Approaching Newaygo, the scenery shifts to forests near the Muskegon River. Following Fremont Street east, M-82 converges with M-37, and together they cross the river into downtown Newaygo on State Street. South of downtown, M-82 splits from M-37, heading east on 82nd Street along the Manistee National Forest's southern edge, ultimately ending at exit 118 on US 131/M-46, west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) regularly tracks traffic flow on its roadways as part of standard upkeep, employing average annual daily traffic (AADT) as a measure. AADT reflects the average number of vehicles traveling a particular section of road each day over the course of a year. MDOT's 2009 figures indicated that M-82 experienced its heaviest traffic west of Fremont, with a daily count of 16,532 vehicles. Conversely, the lightest traffic was observed east of Newaygo, with 4,018 vehicles per day. Additionally, M-82 is not part of the National Highway System, a network of roads considered vital to the country's economy, defense, and general transportation needs.

Designated in 1926, the M-82 highway originally linked US 31 in Hart to the US 131/M-46 intersection in Howard City, traversing Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont via the old M-41. In late 1936, M-46 was extended from Newaygo to Howard City, resulting in a brief concurrency with M-82 to complete a gap in M-46. This overlap ceased in 1938 when M-82 was shortened to its northern intersection with M-37 in Newaygo, leaving the former shared segment as solely M-46. In late 1947 or early 1948, M-82 was rerouted west of Ferry, diverting it westward to Shelby instead of continuing northwest to Hart.

The highway's western segment was realigned twice in the early 1960s, shifting its course from Hesperia to New Era and avoiding Ferry. A more substantial alteration took place around 1969, involving a reshuffling of highway routes in Oceana County. At that time, M-20 took over M-82 west of Hesperia, ending in New Era rather than Muskegon. Simultaneously, M-120 replaced M-20 south of Hesperia, and M-82 was shortened to run only between Hesperia and Newaygo. In 1973, the highway was extended by shifting the eastern end back to Howard City. This change involved rerouting M-46 onto the US 131 freeway to Cedar Springs and replacing M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This allowed the Newaygo to Howard City segment to be redesignated as M-82. The last modification happened in 1978, when the shared section with M-120 was eliminated in favor of M-120. As a result, M-82 was cut back to the junction west of Fremont, defining the route as it exists today.

Masashi Kishimoto created Shikamaru Nara as a character for his Naruto manga and anime. He is a ninja from Konohagakure and part of Team 10, alongside Choji Akimichi, Ino Yamanaka, and their mentor Asuma Sarutobi. Shikamaru is portrayed as lazy and reluctant to utilize his exceptional intelligence. Kishimoto has stated he appreciates Shikamaru's laid-back nature. In addition to the main Naruto storyline, Shikamaru has appeared in four Naruto films and various spin-offs, including video games and original video animations (OVAs).

Shikamaru's persona is a recurring topic in anime and manga media. Commentators commonly emphasize his intellect and laziness, alongside his progression into a leadership position. Anime News Network celebrated Shikamaru's transformation into what they described as "an unlikely hero" in the Naruto story. His appeal resonates with Naruto enthusiasts, as evidenced by his consistently strong performance in popularity polls. Moreover, Shikamaru's image is utilized in diverse merchandise, including figurines, keychains, and emblems.

Masashi Kishimoto admires Shikamaru's laid-back attitude, which he finds appealing given the character's exceptional intelligence, a trait he contrasts with Sasuke Uchiha's keen but less agreeable nature. Kishimoto playfully remarked that, were he a woman, he would marry Shikamaru, confident in his potential for success. In designing Shikamaru's appearance for Part II, Kishimoto sought a unique look, incorporating a standard vest but positioning the forehead protector on Shikamaru's arm to ensure his hairstyle remained prominent.

Shikamaru is first seen in the Chunin Exams, a competition held every two years for ninjas aiming to climb the ranks. He's part of Team 10, alongside Choji Akimichi and Ino Yamanaka. Characterized by his apathetic nature, Shikamaru prefers to do as little as possible. However, beneath his lazy exterior lies extraordinary intelligence; his teacher, Asuma Sarutobi, estimated his IQ to be over 200. Shikamaru's primary skill is the Shadow Imitation Technique (Kagemane no Jutsu), a signature ability of his clan. This technique allows him to fuse his shadow with an enemy's, restricting their movement and forcing them to copy his movements. As the story progresses, Shikamaru develops new ways to control his shadow. By Part II, he can use several shadow techniques at once and even lift his shadow off the ground to interact with physical objects, such as using shadow tendrils to stab enemies or propel weapons.

Shikamaru initially shows a lack of interest in the exams, and despite winning his battle against Temari, he forfeits due to low chakra levels. Despite this, he distinguishes himself as the only ninja from his cohort to be promoted to Chunin. This promotion was largely due to the exceptional intelligence and analytical skills he demonstrated during his fight with Temari, which impressed the exam proctors. Following his promotion, Shikamaru leads a team to prevent Sasuke Uchiha from defecting to Otogakure. Although Shikamaru's squad overcomes the Otogakure ninja sent to intercept them, they ultimately fail to stop Sasuke.

In Part II, Shikamaru is assigned to track down two Akatsuki members, but the immortal [Name] fatally wounds Asuma Sarutobi in battle despite Shikamaru's intervention. Following Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru leads Team 10 and Kakashi Hatake to avenge their fallen teacher. While his comrades face [Name]'s partner, [Name], Shikamaru defeats [Name], ensuring his demise and avenging Asuma. After the fight, Shikamaru vows to safeguard Kurenai [Surname] and Asuma's child. Later, he joins the Fourth Division alongside Temari and [Name], acting as a strategic advisor under Gaara. In the series' conclusion, Shikamaru realizes his long-held desire by marrying Temari, fathering [Name] Nara, and becoming the advisor to the Seventh Hokage, Naruto.

Shikamaru appears in seven Naruto films in addition to the anime and manga series. In the second film, he aids Naruto and Sakura in their battle against Haido, who seeks world domination through a special ability. He briefly engages stone soldiers in combat in the fourth film. In the fifth film, he collaborates with Kakashi and Sai to find the Land of Sky's base, as they plot to invade Konoha. Shikamaru, Sakura, and Sai face a chimera summoned by Hiruko in the sixth film, and he fights the demon Satori in the eighth film. The ninth film presents an alternate reality where Shikamaru is overweight, while his teammate assumes his strategist role. In the tenth film, Shikamaru leads a team to rescue Hanabi Hyuga from an unspecified Otsutsuki. He also competes in a tournament in the third original video animation. Moreover, Shikamaru is a playable character in nearly all Naruto video games, including the Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series, sometimes employing unique versions of his Shadow Imitation Technique. His Part II design was first seen in Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2.

In *Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness*, Takashi Yano tells the story of Shikamaru, illustrated by Kishimoto, who also serves as the protagonist. Set two years after the Fourth Great Ninja War, the novel focuses on Shikamaru's position as leader of the newly formed Allied Shinobi Forces. His task is to apprehend a rogue ninja controlling the isolated Land of Silence, who seeks to establish a new world order ruled by the common people. Furthermore, the story explores the growing relationship between Shikamaru and Temari, foreshadowing his later struggles with naming their future child.

Shikamaru's sustained popularity in the *Naruto* franchise is reflected in his repeated top-ten placements in Weekly Shōnen Jump surveys, including a fourth-place finish. He ranked ninth in the final 2011 poll, coming after Sasori but before Hinata. His widespread appeal has spurred the creation of numerous merchandise items like action figures, keychains, and patches showcasing his appearances in both Part I and Part II. Further proof of his popularity is his ranking as the sixteenth most-liked black-haired male anime character by NTT customers. Hiroshi Matsuyama, the CEO of CyberConnect2, has also voiced his fondness for Shikamaru, naming him as a personal favorite from *Naruto*.

Shikamaru's character has been widely recognized across manga, anime, video games, and associated media. IGN celebrated him as a standout character, calling him the quintessential Generation X representative due to his apathy and reluctance to exert himself. In their review of episode 110, IGN commended Shikamaru's overcoming his laziness to lead the Sasuke retrieval squad, affirming the validity of his Chunin rank. Anime News Network concurred, emphasizing his development into an "unlikely hero" as a significant strength of the storyline. Subsequently, reviewing episode 135 following the mission's failure and the team's injuries, IGN lauded the touching scene of Shikamaru's tears upon hearing of his friends' recovery, anticipating his maturation into an exceptional leader. Justin Rich of Mania Entertainment lauded Shikamaru's "sheer intellect," regarding him as "one of the most fascinating characters" and "one of the few truly brilliant fighters in shōnen anime." Another Mania Entertainment reviewer, Dani Moure, singled out his Chunin Exams fight against Temari as "one of the better fights involving the supporting players."

As the sixth-largest city in Mississippi and the county seat of Lauderdale County, Meridian is the principal city of the Meridian Micropolitan Statistical Area. Its location along important transportation corridors places it strategically: 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Established in 1860 where the Mobile and Ohio Railroad met the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian prospered as a key commercial center due to its railway-driven economy and the transportation of goods. The city endured significant destruction during the American Civil War, particularly in February 1864, when General William Tecumseh Sherman's troops destroyed a considerable part of Meridian in the Battle of Meridian.

After rebuilding from the war, the city entered a "Golden Age," becoming Mississippi's largest city between 1890 and 1930 and a significant manufacturing center in the South, supported by 44 trains daily. Union Station, built in 1906, is now a multi-modal center for transportation, connecting passengers to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, serving around 242,360 passengers each year. Although the city faced economic challenges with the decline of the railroad industry, it has since broadened its economic base, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing as the primary employers in 2010. In 2008, the city's population was approximately 38,232, but its economy draws from a workforce of 104,600 within a 45-mile radius (total population 232,900) and 234,200 within a 65-mile radius (total population 526,500).

Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field significantly bolster the regional economy, together contributing over 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian is home to both the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and Mississippi's first Department of Homeland Security office. Key Field, named after Fred and Al Key, who set a flight endurance world record in 1935, currently hosts the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support facility for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. The largest non-military employer in the region is Rush Foundation Hospital, which employs 2,610 people.

Meridian is known for its thriving arts community and deep historical roots, reflected in prominent cultural institutions such as the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The city's past includes two Carnegie libraries, which were segregated. Of these, the Carnegie Branch Library, now demolished, was one of many libraries created for African Americans in the South during the segregation era.

Meridian will be home to the forthcoming Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center ( <unk> ). As the birthplace of Jimmie Rodgers, the "Father of Country Music," the city's Highland Park houses a museum dedicated to his life and work, displaying related artifacts alongside steam-era railroad relics. The park is also home to the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a unique National Historic Landmark recognized as the world's only surviving two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie. Meridian's notable natives include Miss America 1986 Susan Akin, civil rights activist James Chaney, who was murdered in the 1964 Mississippi killings, and Hartley Peavey, founder of Meridian-based Peavey Electronics. The city's federal courthouse was the venue for the 1966-1967 trial concerning Chaney's murder and two other activists, a landmark case where a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights-related homicide for the first time.

The area now known as Meridian was originally inhabited by the Choctaw people. In 1830, the United States gained control of this land through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, a component of the Indian Removal period. After the treaty was ratified, European-American settlers began to move into the area.

Richard McLemore, the first person to settle in Meridian, encouraged development by donating portions of his approximately 2,000-acre federal land grant to attract new residents. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer from Alabama, bought most of McLemore's land, and John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County, bought the remaining 80 acres. Ragsdale and Ball, recognized as the city's founders, then started dividing their property into plots for building.

The settlement's naming was a contentious issue. Ball and the city's industrial workers supported "Meridian," viewing it as equivalent to "junction," whereas the farming community preferred "<unk>," a Native American phrase meaning "mad river" taken from a nearby creek. Ragsdale even proposed "Ragsdale City." To satisfy both factions, Ball rotated the "Meridian" and "<unk>" signs each day at his Mobile and Ohio Railroad station. Eventually, the expanding railroad industry drew in more laborers who favored "Meridian," solidifying it as the station's permanent name. The town was formally incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

Meridian began as a small village, but its importance as a railroad hub early in the Civil War led the Confederacy to establish military installations there. In 1864, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman's forces attacked Meridian, destroying railroads, an arsenal, and extensive warehouses in every direction. A large number of buildings were also burned. Sherman is said to have declared that Meridian, with its depots, warehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments, was essentially destroyed. Despite this devastation, the city's railway network was rapidly rebuilt and back in service within 26 working days. The period of Reconstruction that followed was marked by ongoing racial strife, which eventually led to the riot of 1871 after a fire damaged many businesses.

The town prospered after the Civil War, experiencing its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. Railroads improved accessibility and drew in businesses, resulting in a surge in population. This growth fueled commercial development in the downtown area. Between 1890 and 1930, Meridian rose to become Mississippi's largest city and a significant manufacturing center in the South. Many landmark buildings, including the Grand Opera House (1890), Wechsler School (1894), two Carnegie libraries (1913), and the <unk> Building (1929), Meridian's tallest skyscraper, were erected during and shortly after this era.

The city continued to grow, driven by a commission government that secured 90 new industrial plants in 1913 and a flourishing automobile industry in the 1920s. Even after the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, the city remained attractive to new businesses. As escapism became popular during the Depression's worst years, downtown Meridian saw the opening of the S. H. Kress & Co. building, intended to "provide luxury to the common man," and the Temple Theater, which operated as a movie house. In 1933, the federal courthouse was erected as a Works Progress Administration (WPA) project.

The railroad industry experienced a resurgence during World War II, rebounding from a post-Depression slump. Meridian once again became a key regional rail center, as trains were essential for moving vital resources such as gasoline and scrap metal needed for manufacturing military vehicles. This boom continued until the 1950s, when the rise of cars and the developing Interstate Highway System diminished the importance of passenger trains. The resulting decline in the railroad industry caused significant job losses and population decrease as workers looked for employment in other fields.

During the 1960s Civil Rights Movement, Meridian, Mississippi, was an important hub, housing a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office and serving as a base for various activist groups. James Chaney, along with Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, Andrew Goodman, and local community members, worked together to create a community center and provide voter education for African Americans. This activism provoked anger among local white residents, resulting in repeated acts of racial violence. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman went to Neshoba County to investigate the arson of a black church. On their drive back to Meridian that evening, they disappeared. A massive FBI investigation followed, leading to the discovery of their remains two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

The trial for the murders of civil rights workers in Mississippi, held at the Meridian federal courthouse, saw an all-white jury convict seven Klansmen, including a deputy sheriff, for violating the victims' civil rights, while acquitting three others. This was the first time a white official was convicted by a white jury in a civil rights killing. Decades later, in 2005, the state reopened the case, leading to Edgar Ray Killen's manslaughter conviction and a 60-year prison term. Afterward, Meridian honored Chaney by renaming a portion of 49th Avenue after him and creating a yearly memorial service.

The building of highways in the 1960s, making commutes easier, encouraged people to move from the city's core to new northern suburbs. As businesses started leaving downtown, the city reacted by creating historic districts in the 1970s and 80s to preserve its distinctive architecture. This initiative resulted in the establishment of the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission in 1979 and the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street led several efforts to revitalize downtown, including the construction of a new Amtrak station in 1997. This station was intentionally modeled after Meridian's original, now-demolished, historic train station from its heyday. Other projects involved renovating the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, as well as encouraging overall urban planning. In 2006, Meridian Main Street partnered with The Riley Foundation to renovate the historic Grand Opera House, converting it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

After the Alliance for Downtown Meridian acquired Meridian Main Street in late 2007, a joint revitalization effort began, spearheaded by the Alliance, Meridian Main Street, and the Meridian Downtown Association. The Alliance acts as a core support system, offering staffing, office space, and communication channels to the other two groups. Despite initial intentions to rehabilitate a building, these plans were suspended by Mayor Cheri Barry in early 2010. Presently, the Alliance prioritizes downtown growth and refurbishment, aiming to draw niche retailers, eateries, and bars to invigorate both day and night life. Simultaneously, the Meridian Downtown Association works to increase foot traffic via special events, and Meridian Main Street is committed to bolstering the current businesses in the downtown area.

Meridian's role as a central railroad junction led to a boom in hotel construction to meet the needs of passengers. Prior to its peak, notable establishments such as the Great Southern and Grand Avenue hotels were already in place before the turn of the century. With railroad growth and the opening of the original Union Station in 1906, more hotels arose to cater to both travelers and railway staff. The Elmira Hotel opened its doors in 1905, with the Terminal Hotel following in 1910. Hotel Meridian was founded in 1907, and the Union Hotel in 1908. The Union Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were later designated as contributing properties within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

The city's thriving economy spurred the expansion of its hotel industry, highlighted by the construction of the eleven-story Lamar Hotel in 1927. Reflecting the city's ambitions, this structure was included on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. Subsequently, the Lamar Hotel was converted into a county annex building and designated a Mississippi Landmark in 1988.

The E.F. Young Hotel, built in 1931, was central to the thriving African American commercial area located west of downtown. In the period of segregation, it was a rare haven in the city, offering accommodation to African American travelers when few other places would.

After suburban growth in the 1960s and 70s led to hotels moving out of the city center, the 2006 Riley Center renovation created a need for a new downtown hotel. Although redeveloping the <unk> Building was proposed to fulfill this need, changes in city government slowed down the restoration. As a result, the <unk> Preservation Society was formed in 2013 to promote the building's renovation through public tours of the ground floor and special events.

Meridian is home to nine historically important districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places. One of these, the Meridian Downtown Historic District, combines the previous Meridian Urban Center Historic District with the Union Station Historic District. These areas display a wide variety of architectural styles popular from the late 19th to the early 20th centuries, including Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow.
