Meridian has operated under a "strong mayor" system since 1985. In this structure, the city's voters choose a mayor every four years. Simultaneously, each of the five city wards, represented as individual districts, elects a city council member who also serves a four-year term. The mayor, as the chief executive, manages the city government's daily operations and provides leadership. The city council, on the other hand, functions as the legislative branch, tasked with creating policies and approving the annual city budget.

City Hall, a nationally recognized historic landmark situated at 601 23rd Avenue, is currently led by Mayor Percy Bland. The city council includes Dr. George M. Thomas representing Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham of Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston of Ward 4, and Randy Hammon of Ward 5. Pam McInnis fulfills the duties of council clerk, and the city employs a total of 570 individuals.

Following Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city established a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), becoming the only local DHS in Mississippi and taking charge of a nine-county area. Supported by $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other sources, the department launched passenger rail rescue training for law enforcement officers from other Southern states. It also offers public courses in handgun basics, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms. The DHS is vital in crisis management, evidenced by its support in establishing and operating shelters for 700 evacuees during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005. The city now heads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which consists of three teams, each overseeing nine counties.

Under the leadership of Chief Lee <unk> since 2009, the Meridian Police Department staffs 115 full-time officers, complemented by part-time and reserve staff. The department's Criminal Investigations Division managed 4,000 cases in 2009, with felonies accounting for 50% of the total. Reported <unk> crimes in 2000 marginally exceeded the number of incidents recorded in 2008. Meridian is recognized as "the safest city in Mississippi with more than 30,000 people." Located in unincorporated Lauderdale County, near Meridian, is the East Mississippi Correctional Facility, operated by the GEO Group on behalf of the Mississippi Department of Corrections. The Meridian Fire Department, headed by Chief Anthony Clayton, responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, including 123 structure fires and 609 emergency service calls.

The city is apportioned into three districts for the Mississippi Senate. Senator Terry Clark Burton (R) presides over the 31st District, encompassing the northernmost section. The 32nd District, represented by Senator Sampson Jackson, II (D), stretches from the southwest to the northeast. Senator <unk> Carmichael (R) represents the 33rd District, which includes the western and southeastern portions. In the Mississippi House, the city is divided into four districts. Representative Steven A. Horne (R) serves District 81, covering the southern and eastern regions. Representative Wilbert L. Jones (D) represents District 82, which is entirely within the city's center. District 83, surrounding District 82, is represented by Representative Greg Snowden (R). Representative Tad Campbell (R) represents District 84, covering the western and a small northern part of the city.

Meridian, Mississippi is part of the 3rd congressional district, currently represented by Republican Gregg Harper, who has held the seat since 2009. Lauderdale County, the home of Meridian, has reliably voted for Republican presidential candidates since 1972. Prior to this, white voters in the county traditionally backed Democratic candidates, mirroring Mississippi's entrenched one-party Democratic rule that lasted for many decades, starting in the late 1800s.

Social and economic factors have intricately influenced the city's growth patterns. Initially, the city's population consistently increased between its founding and 1970, although the rate of growth varied considerably, from a peak of 165% to a minimal 0.02%. A population decline was noted in the 1970 census, with a small recovery by 1980. Afterward, the city's population gradually decreased before increasing again in the 2000s. Between 1980 and 2000, the population shrunk by more than 14%. The 2000 census indicated a population of 39,968 and a density of 885.9 residents per square mile (342.0/km2). By 2008, the city was the state's sixth largest, and its population was still growing as of 2010.

Meridian functions as the core of its micropolitan area, which includes Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale counties and had an estimated population of 106,139 in 2009. The city's reach goes beyond this immediate area, impacting a region containing 232,900 people within a 45-mile radius and 526,500 individuals within a 65-mile radius.

Even with changes in the city's overall population, the number and percentage of non-white residents have steadily grown, except for a period between 1960 and 1970 when the city's total population decreased substantially. The 2010 Census data revealed the city's racial makeup to be: 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% belonging to other racial groups, and 0.89% identifying as two or more races. Furthermore, those of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, irrespective of race, made up 1.75% of the city's inhabitants.

According to the 2000 Census, the city contained 17,890 housing units, of which 15,966 were occupied. Among the occupied units, 10,033 were family households. These households included 31.1% with children under 18, 36.2% that were married couples, and 23.3% headed by women with no husband present. Non-family households accounted for 37.2% of the total. Individuals living alone made up 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% had a resident aged 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.39, while the average family size was 3.06. It's worth noting that the average household size has declined from 3.04 in 1970. Concurrently, the median age in Meridian increased from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The city's economic profile reveals a median household income of $25,085 and a median family income of $31,062. Men had a median income of $29,404, exceeding the $19,702 median for women. The per capita income in the city was $15,255. A significant portion of the population experienced poverty, with 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the total population below the poverty line. This included a disproportionately high percentage of children under 18 (40.8%) and seniors aged 65 and over (22.0%).

Religious participation in Meridian and its vicinity is significantly above the national norm. Around 65.2% of Lauderdale County's population are affiliated with a religious body, exceeding the national average of 50.2%. Data from 2000 indicates that Southern Baptists were the most prevalent denomination, accounting for 30,068 members (59.0%), with the United Methodist Church following at 9,469 members (18.6%), and the Catholic Church with 1,872 members (3.7%).

German and Eastern European Jewish immigrants played a vital role in Meridian's economic development through the creation of diverse businesses and services. The establishment of Congregation Beth Israel in 1868 occurred before the city's thriving "Golden Age." By 1927, Meridian's Jewish community was the largest in Mississippi, numbering 575 people. Today, however, the Jewish population has decreased to under 40, largely composed of older individuals.

Located in Lauderdale County, Meridian resides in the North Central Hills region of Mississippi. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the city encompasses a total area of 45.9 square miles (119 square kilometers), of which 45.1 square miles (117 square kilometers) is land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 square kilometers) is water. Benefitting from its location on major highways, Meridian is located 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 kilometers) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding terrain consists of cotton and corn fields mingled with oak and pine forests, defined by clay hills and the low-lying areas that supply the source waters of the [River Name].

The city's downtown area has been reshaped by construction, but the outskirts maintain a softly rolling topography. Numerous small creeks are dispersed throughout the city, and both the northern and southern boundaries are characterized by small lakes and wooded tracts. A significant stream, <unk> Creek, cuts across the southern portion of the city, dividing into Gallagher's Creek as it passes through the city center. Loper's Creek winds along the city's westernmost edge, while several minor streams, including Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are found in various locations within the city.

Meridian is characterized by a humid subtropical climate. Summer, spanning from June to August, sees average high temperatures around 90°F (32°C) and average lows near 70°F (21°C). Winter, occurring between December and February, has average highs of approximately 60°F (16°C) and average lows dropping to about 35°F (2°C). The hottest month is usually July, with an average high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), while January is the coldest, averaging a low of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

Year-round, the city experiences fairly consistent rainfall, totaling an average of 58 to 65 inches (1,490 mm) annually. The month with the highest rainfall is March, with an average of 6.93 inches (176 mm). Thunderstorms are common, especially in the summer, adding considerably to the precipitation and potentially occurring in any season. Severe thunderstorms, which can produce damaging winds, large hail, lightning, and intense rainfall, happen occasionally, mainly in the spring and, to a smaller degree, in the fall, and can also bring the threat of tornadoes.

The local economy initially depended significantly on railroads. At the beginning of the 20th century, the city was Mississippi's largest, featuring five major rail lines and handling 44 trains daily. The city's economic power was linked to both the railroads and the goods they carried, including timber and cotton. These rail-dependent sectors made the city a major economic player in the state and surrounding area from about 1890 to 1930. While the railroad industry's decline in the 1950s led to an economic downturn, the city has shifted from a mainly rail-centered economy to a more diverse one, with healthcare, the military, and manufacturing now being the main sources of employment.

The East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, founded in 1996 by local entrepreneurs, serves Meridian, Lauderdale County, and Marion. Although Meridian's civilian workforce was just 15,420 in April 2010, its location allows it to function as a hub for jobs, shopping, medical services, and cultural activities. This is due to a larger labor market of 104,600 within a 45-mile (72 km) area (with a total population of 232,900) and 234,200 within a 65-mile (105 km) area (total population of 526,500). A significant portion of Lauderdale County's workforce lives locally, with 80% residing within the county and 90% within a 45-mile radius.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County's healthcare industry provided 6,260 jobs. Rush Hospital was the largest employer in this sector, employing 2,610 individuals, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500 and Anderson Hospital with 1,475 employees. Meridian contains three hospitals and numerous other healthcare facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers cardiovascular surgery, a Level II NICU, and a health and fitness center. Rush Foundation Hospital, along with Rush Health Systems, operates the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing long-term hospital care for patients needing extended recovery. Riley Hospital includes specialized stroke and rehabilitation centers. Other healthcare providers in Meridian include Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has served the community since 1882.

As of April 2010, retail was a major employer in the county, providing jobs for 5,280 people. The city's retail sector generates roughly $2 billion annually. Bonita Lakes Mall, encompassing 633,685 square feet (58,871 m2), offers over 100 stores and services, including department stores, specialty shops, restaurants, and a United Artists Theatres. The retail environment was also boosted by the November 2007 completion of Phase I of Meridian Crossroads, a 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m2) shopping center located in the Bonita Lakes area. In addition, the North Hills Street shopping district has expanded, and more retail and office space was developed near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

Two military facilities, Naval Air Station (NAS) Meridian and Key Field, provide over 4,000 jobs for Meridian residents. NAS Meridian is a training site for naval carrier pilots and enlisted staff and is home to the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy, which provides narcotics training for law enforcement across several southeastern states. Meridian also hosts the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, which manages a regional response team covering nine counties and a regional response task force spanning twenty-nine counties. Key Field, famous for the 1935 record-breaking endurance flight of Fred and Al Key, now houses the Air National Guard's 186th Air Refueling Wing and a support facility for the Army National Guard's 185th Aviation Brigade. Additionally, Key Field is the site of an aviation history display and Meridian's Aviation Museum.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County's manufacturing industries provided jobs for 2,850 people. The city serves as the home base for Peavey Electronics Corporation, a long-standing manufacturer of guitars, amplifiers, and audio equipment since its establishment in 1965. In addition to Peavey, Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation all maintain a business presence in the region, which also features four industrial parks.

The MSU Riley Center, located in downtown Meridian, stimulates the local economy by attracting tourists and providing a venue for arts and entertainment. Annually, it brings more than 60,000 visitors to the city's core for events like conferences, meetings, and diverse shows. Loeb's Department Store, a historic Mississippi clothing retailer on Front Street, remains a family-run business now in its fourth generation. Founded in 1887 by Alex Loeb, the store has consistently offered premium clothing for both men and women.

For over 100 years, Meridian has cultivated a thriving arts scene, fostering many cultural organizations and a lively schedule of events. The Meridian Art League, a foundational group, began in 1933, initially hosting exhibitions at the Lamar Hotel. In 1949, it became the Meridian Art Association and moved its shows to various locations. When the Carnegie Library closed, the Association renovated the building at 25th Ave and 7th St, establishing the Meridian Museum of Art as a permanent exhibition space. Since its opening in 1970, the museum has offered diverse temporary exhibits and educational opportunities for all ages. It hosts over 30 exhibitions each year, displaying everything from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic items, photography, crafts, and various other art forms. The museum also maintains a collection of 18th- and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photographs, and sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA), founded in 1978, functions as the designated arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County. The MCA administers the Community Art Grants program, the annual Threefoot Festival, workshops, and other special events. It partners with arts organizations in the area, including the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, built in 1932 and one of the South's oldest subscription-based community theaters, draws over 22,000 local and visiting patrons each season, making it Mississippi's most popular community theater. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra, established in 1961, debuted in concert in 1962 and presented its first full season in 1963. In 1965, the Orchestra featured its first international soloist, Elena Nikolaidi. The Orchestra aided the Meridian Public School District in starting its orchestra and strings programs and helped create the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard has been the conductor since 1991. The Orchestra celebrated its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House, built in 1889 by Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, quickly became a celebrated performance space, hosting famous artists and productions, starting with a German company's rendition of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron." The opera house closed in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression and sat abandoned for nearly seventy years. In 2000, a $10 million gift from the Riley Foundation, a local group founded in 1998, launched its restoration, supported by $15 million in city, state, and federal grants. The opera house's renovation was completed in September 2006, and it reopened as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." Boasting a 950-seat theater for live performances, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 square meters) of conference space, the center attracts over 60,000 visitors annually to downtown Meridian for events like conferences, meetings, and shows.

Meridian is renowned for its architectural significance, showcasing a remarkably intact array of early 20th-century buildings that attract architecture students from across North America. Among its treasures is the sole Southern residence by Louis S. Curtiss, the innovative designer of glass curtain wall skyscrapers, located in Highland Park. The Frank Fort Building is acclaimed as a quintessential Art Deco skyscraper, rivaling Detroit's Fisher Building in design excellence. California's Wallace Neff, with family ties to the local railroad industry, also contributed to Meridian's architectural landscape, along with Alabama's Black Belt, designing homes during lulls in his California practice. His work, mainly found on Poplar Springs Drive, bears resemblance to his design of Rudolph Valentino's Falcon Lair, though two of his Meridian creations have been lost. The Meridian Post Office, an extravagant structure adorned with bronze and Verde marble, exemplifies the lavish post offices built in thriving cities during the 1920s. Its original lighting fixtures, removed during a 1960s renovation, now grace private residences on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian is planned as the location for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center (MAEC). The Mississippi Legislature approved the idea in 2001 and promised $4 million in 2006, contingent on securing $8 million in private funding. The city then provided $50,000 in September 2007. The MAEC project envisions a 175-acre (71 ha) area at Bonita Lakes, complete with an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert venue, and a Hall of Fame celebrating Mississippi artists. The Hall of Fame itself will be located downtown in the old Montana's building, purchased along with the neighboring Meridian Hotel building for $300,000 in July 2010. To build anticipation for the Hall of Fame, the MAEC launched its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center in February 2009. The first star recognized Meridian native Jimmie Rodgers, followed by one for Mississippi blues icon B.B. King in September of that year. On June 1, 2010, Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, and William Faulkner were added to the Walk, with Sela Ward joining on June 24, 2010. The MAEC plans to feature many other Mississippi-born luminaries on the Walk of Fame, including Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, and Conway Twitty.

The Temple Theater, situated in the local Shrine Temple, is a significant performance space notable for its 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, a unique theater organ still in its original state. With an initial seating capacity of 1,800, it flourished during the silent film period, becoming one of the nation's largest stages, surpassed only by New York City's Roxy Theater. Today, with a capacity of 1,576, the Temple Theater presents diverse events year-round, such as live performances, plays, concerts, Shrine functions, and public screenings of classic movies.

Located in Highland Park, the Jimmie Rodgers Museum exhibits the legendary "Singing Brakeman's" original guitar, personal and professional memorabilia, and railroad artifacts from the steam era. The museum grounds also feature outdoor tributes and a classic steam locomotive. In Meridian, Rodgers' birthplace, a Mississippi Blues Trail marker acknowledges his pivotal role in Mississippi blues, a first for a location outside the Delta. Additionally, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker honoring Rodgers was placed at Oak Grove Cemetery on June 1, 2010. The city has also celebrated his life with a yearly festival every May since 1953, marking the anniversary of his passing.

Highland Park is also home to the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a National Historic Landmark. This carousel, made around 1895 by Gustav Dentzel, is unique as the only remaining two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. It has been running since 1909 and its building is the only one still standing that was built using Dentzel's original blueprints. The "Around Town" public art project features 62 carousel horse sculptures, each representing the historic carousel. These sculptures, sponsored by local businesses and community members and designed and painted by local artists, are exhibited throughout the city and county.

The city offers a range of recreational areas, including Highland Park, Bonita Lakes, and another significant lake. Highland Park is open throughout the year and features picnic shelters, swimming pools, tennis courts, a baseball diamond, softball fields, and a children's playground. Bonita Lakes, a 3,300-acre city park (13 km2), encompasses three lakes, the Long Creek Reservoir, and the Lakeview Municipal Golf Course. Visitors can also enjoy nature trails, a jogging/walking path, cycling trails, horseback riding paths, pavilions, picnic areas, boat ramps, paddle boats, food vendors, and fishing. The Bonita Lakes area also includes the Bonita Lakes Mall, Bonita Lakes Crossing, and Bonita Lakes Plaza. The unnamed lake, covering 7,150 acres (28.9 km2), includes a 4,144-acre (16.77 km2) lake ideal for boating, fishing, swimming, water skiing, picnicking, hunting, hiking, and camping. Located on the lake's property are Splashdown Country Water Park, a 25-room motel, and cabins.

Since 1992, Meridian has been the venue for the State Games of Mississippi, a yearly, Olympic-style, statewide sports competition. As a member of the National Congress of State Games, the organization maintains ties with the U.S. Olympic Committee. The first games involved 1,200 athletes competing in a dozen sports, and participation has since expanded to include over 70,000 athletes. In 2009, more than 4,500 athletes competed across 27 sports. All participants qualify for the Southeast Sports Festival, and medalists have the opportunity to compete in the State Games of America, held every two years.

The games, originally a single weekend event in June, expanded to two weekends to accommodate more sports. The opening ceremonies are a long-standing tradition, starting on the third Friday of June in downtown Meridian. Sporting events take place at several locations throughout the city, including Northeast Park and the Davidson Complex. Northeast Park, a large 85-acre space on Highway 39, offers ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, an asphalt track, and a large picnic area. As an Amtrak Crescent line station, Meridian offers convenient links to metropolises like New York City, Philadelphia, and New Orleans. Located at 1901 Front Street in the Meridian Downtown Historic District, the Union Station Multi-Modal Transportation Center acts as a central point for diverse modes of transportation. Originally built in 1906, the station was reconstructed in 1997 following its demolition in 1966. Today, it hosts the Meridian Transit System, Amtrak, the Norfolk Southern rail line, Greyhound and Trailways buses, and other transportation services, collectively facilitating approximately 242,360 passenger trips each year via Amtrak, Greyhound, and Meridian Transit buses.

Key Field, also known as Meridian Regional Airport and located on Airport Boulevard South, serves the city with air transportation. The airport is positioned 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of downtown Meridian and features Mississippi's longest public runway, extending 10,004 feet (3,049 m). In operation since 1930, it offers daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth, Texas.

During the Great Depression, the city contemplated shutting down the airport because of maintenance costs. But in 1935, airport administrators Fred and Al Key came up with a scheme to rescue it. The brothers flew their aircraft, the "Ole Miss," non-stop above the city from June 4 to July 1, 1935. Their 27-day flight, totaling 653 hours and 34 minutes, attracted enough publicity and funds to prevent the airport's closure. As a result, the airport was named Key Field in their honor, acknowledging the Key brothers, whose flight endurance achievement still stands as the longest in conventional aviation.

After the 1870 Mississippi Constitution, Meridian created its first public education system. From 1870 to 1885, the City Council chose trustees for the Board of School Directors, which managed the schools. Before 1884, private schools served only about 400 students. Meridian's first public school building was built in September 1884. The first public school for African American children was held in rented rooms at St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, the Mississippi Legislature amended the city charter, giving Meridian control over its own school district. Shortly after, in March 1888, voters approved $30,000 in bonds to fund the construction of new public schools. One result of this funding was the Wechsler School, built in 1894, which was the first brick public school building in Mississippi built specifically for black students.

The Meridian Public School District has grown from a modest beginning to encompass six elementary, three middle, and three high schools. Alongside the public system, Meridian offers private schooling choices including Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, the district's main secondary institution, occupies a 37-acre (15 ha) site featuring six buildings with 111 classrooms and educates approximately 1,500 students in grades 10 through 12.

Meridian is home to two higher education institutions. Meridian Community College, founded in 1937 at 910 Highway 19 N, offers four free semesters to graduates of Meridian and Lauderdale County schools, including homeschooled students in the county. Originally called Meridian Junior College and located at Meridian High School, it moved to its current location in 1965. After desegregation, it consolidated with T.J. Harris Junior College, previously for African-American students, in 1970. The college was renamed Meridian Community College in 1987 "to better represent the variety of opportunities it offers a growing community." Mississippi State University also has a Meridian campus. In the fall of 2008, the college enrolled 763 students from 33 Mississippi counties and multiple Alabama counties.

The Meridian @-@ Lauderdale County Public Library now stands at 7th Street and 26th Avenue in Meridian. The city previously had two Carnegie libraries, built in 1913 for segregated black and white populations. The Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club, founded in the 1880s by local women, campaigned for a Meridian library, donating their collection to start it. With broad community backing, they engaged city official Israel Marks to secure funding from Andrew Carnegie. The black library was built at 13th Street and 28th Avenue on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church. The white library occupied a building purchased from the First Presbyterian Church of Meridian in 1911. The African American library was Mississippi's only library for blacks until after World War I and the only Carnegie library in the US designed for African Americans. In 1967, following the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the libraries integrated, combining resources at the current location. The former white library became the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970, and the original African American library was demolished on May 28, 2008.

Located west of mainland Shetland, Papa Stour is an 828-hectare (3.2 square miles) island and the eighth largest in the Shetland archipelago, Scotland. Its population is small, numbering less than twenty, including some residents who came to the island through a 1970s recruitment program. The island's delicate volcanic rock has been eroded over time, creating a diverse coastline featuring caves, sea stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. Both Papa Stour and its surrounding waters support a rich variety of wildlife. The island's western shore is a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the marine area around it holds Special Area of Conservation status.

This island boasts several Neolithic burial sites alongside the remains of Duke Hakon's 13th-century home, a remnant of Norse occupation. The population swelled to over 380 in the 19th century due to a fishing station founded at <unk> in West Voe. Following this peak, the population declined consistently before recovering from a low of 16 in the 1970s.

Located off the southwestern edge of St Magnus Bay, Papa Stour features a striking 34-kilometer (21-mile) coastline characterized by numerous small inlets and four prominent voes (bays). Housa Voe, meaning "harbor bay" in Old Norse and situated in the south, provides the most sheltered anchorage, with a natural rock arch adorning its nearby cliffs. On the eastern side, West Voe, whose Old Norse name means "house bay," is more exposed but functions as the island's main harbor and ferry landing.

Holm and Maiden Stack mark the harbor's southern entry. Holm, a tidal island, was once a leper colony until the 1700s, although some speculate that vitamin deficiencies were the true ailment of many inhabitants. Maiden Stack's name comes from a 14th-century legend. The story says Lord Thorvald constructed a small home on its peak, the remnants of which are still visible, to keep his daughter away from men. This plan backfired when she became pregnant after leaving; another account says she and her fisherman lover ran away together successfully. A glacial moraine belt, about 1.5 kilometers in length, bisects the island's western section. The rest of the terrain mainly consists of thin, stony soil, likely derived from glacial till. Remarkably, peat is virtually nonexistent, and the volcanic bedrock contributes to comparatively rich soil. This lack of peat led to turf being stripped for fuel, creating patches of exposed rock in the island's center.

In a move that went unacknowledged by the UK government, Stuart Hill, the only resident and owner of the 2.5-acre Forvik Holm – which he renamed "Forvik Island" – declared its independence on June 21, 2008. He based this declaration and the establishment of the Crown Dependency of Forvik on a 1468 marriage agreement between the kings of Norway and Scotland, arguing the island's rightful status as a British crown dependency independent from both the UK and the EU.

The island's geological makeup comprises a mix of volcanic and sedimentary rocks originating from the Devonian period when Scotland resided within the Old Red Sandstone Continent, positioned between 10 and 25 degrees south of the equator. These Old Red Sandstone deposits, laid down between 408 and 370 million years ago, stemmed from the erosion of older Silurian rocks, elevated during the creation of Pangaea, and their subsequent accumulation in river deltas. The freshwater Lake Orcadie stretched along the margins of these eroding mountains, reaching from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour is largely composed of volcanic ash and lavas from the period's volcanic activity, including hardened layers of volcanic ash and rhyolite lava, along with a Devonian fish bed at Lamba Banks. Furthermore, numerous large boulders were deposited by Pleistocene glacial activity.

The island's soft volcanic rock has been sculpted by marine erosion into a stunning array of geological features, including caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, and voes, regarded as some of the UK's finest examples. The 'Holl o' is a notable cave that pierces the island's northwest tip, extending almost half a mile and wide enough to accommodate rowing. Another significant cave, 'Christie's Hole' in the southwest, is characterized by a partial roof collapse that occurred in 1981. The seas around Papa Stour, and the island itself, are rich in wildlife. Otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises are frequently seen. The island provides nesting habitats for a diverse array of birds, such as Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, Arctic skuas, northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls. Furthermore, Papa Stour attracts numerous migratory birds.

Papa Stour is home to diverse wildflowers, including mountain everlasting, spring squill, and a yet-to-be-identified flower, in addition to the prevalent heather. The island's west coast is a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest, and the sea around it is a Special Area of Conservation. The island also sustains the breeding of native Shetland Ponies.

Human presence on the island dates back to approximately 3000 BC, indicated by the presence of Neolithic "heel-shaped cairns" used for burials. Although details regarding the pre-Celtic and Celtic eras are limited, Norse explorers are thought to have encountered a religious settlement there. The island's name derives from <unk> <unk>, meaning "Big island of the Papar" (Celtic monks), to distinguish it from Papa Little, situated about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

Papa Stour appears in Shetland's earliest surviving document, a 1299 Old Norse manuscript, which details a noteworthy incident at the residence of Duke Hakon Magnusson, later King Hakon V of Norway. Close to <unk> Voe beach, a stone circle denotes the location of a 'ting,' or local gathering place, where Lord Thorvald <unk>, implicated in corruption in the 1299 record and subsequently referred to as ‘dominus de <unk> ’, triumphed in a duel. Although Shetland officially became part of Scotland in 1469, Norwegian landowners retained their Papa Stour properties until the 1600s. In the 16th century, traders from Bremen and Hamburg set up temporary bases to buy fish from the island's fishermen. By the 18th century, the island was in the hands of two Scottish proprietors, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick, who managed a profitable summer haaf (deep sea) fishing business using sixareen vessels.

The island church, built in 1806, overlooks Kirk Sand in Fore Wick Bay. About 300 meters away on the headland dividing Kirk Sand's western edge and a neighboring bay, there may be the remains of an older chapel. This site, called the "blank kirk" locally and labeled by the Ordnance Survey as "the site of a blank chapel dating back to around the twelfth century," is believed to have been plagued by supernatural interference that undid construction work each night. According to legend, these supernatural beings moved the cornerstones to the present church site, allowing its completion. Archaeological excavations in 2004 discovered mostly large rhyolite blocks and a piece of whalebone rib, possibly supporting the local stories.

In the 19th century, the establishment of a fishing station at West Voe spurred a surge in Papa Stour's population, peaking at over 360. Yet, starting in the 1870s, dwindling fish populations due to steam drifters and a shortage of fuel resulted in a population decrease. This period also saw the arrival of Edwin Lindsay, an Indian army officer and the Earl of Balcarres' son, who was exiled to Papa Stour after being declared insane for declining a duel. He spent 26 years in confinement until Quaker preacher Catherine Watson intervened and gained his release in 1835. Lindsay's Well, a spring in the south, commemorates the location where he was allowed to bathe.

Horizontal water mills, also known as Norse or Clack Mills, were frequently found close to Dutch Loch. Characteristically, these mills were two-storied buildings with turf roofs, constructed into hillsides to provide entry to the upper floor housing the millstone. Inside, a fixed lower millstone worked in conjunction with a rotating upper millstone, driven by water striking paddles underneath. A few of these mills continued to operate on Papa Stour until the beginning of the 20th century, and a working model can still be seen on the Burn of [location], at [location] in southern Mainland Shetland.

Papa Stour, like other small Scottish islands, experienced a population boom in the 19th century before a significant decline, mirroring the fate of Mingulay. The island's school closed in 1970, leaving only sixteen "fairly elderly" residents. A turning point came with an Exchange and Mart ad offering a free croft and five sheep, which attracted many applicants and boosted the population to 33 by 1981. However, internal disputes and legal issues led to a decrease to 20 by 2005, triggering further emigration and the school's renewed closure. By early 2008, only nine inhabitants remained after a family of seven left. Despite this, the 2011 census recorded 15 permanent residents, contrasting with an overall 4% increase in Scottish island populations to 103,702 between 2001 and 2011.

On March 28, 1930, the Aberdeen-based trawler Ben Doran wrecked on the Ve Skerries, situated 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, as it sailed toward Scalloway to offload its catch. Despite initially good weather, the wreck went unnoticed until a trawler spotted and reported it the following day. By then, the weather had deteriorated, hindering rescue attempts by the coastguard and local volunteers, as Shetland lacked a lifeboat then. A plea for assistance was sent to the Stromness lifeboat in Orkney, a mere 120 miles distant, but help arrived too late. Sadly, all nine crew members perished in the disaster. Only three bodies were found: James Mitchell, who was repatriated to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R. <unk>, who were laid to rest in Scalloway.

In February 1940, dense fog caused the cargo vessel SS Highcliffe to be wrecked on <unk> Holm. The weather conditions, aside from the fog, were fortunately mild, resulting in the loss of only the ship and its goods. Subsequently, in 1967, the Aberdeen-based trawler Juniper ran aground in Lyra Sound, at the foot of towering 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The <unk> lifeboat team successfully saved all 12 crewmen, and the coxswain received the RNLI silver medal in recognition of his courageous actions.

On December 9, 1977, the trawler Elinor Viking from Aberdeen, skippered by Alec Flett, became the latest vessel to be wrecked near Papa Stour, running aground on the Ve Skerries. The local lifeboat was unable to reach the crew due to treacherous seas. Consequently, Alec Webster, the Lerwick Coastguard Station Officer, called for help, and a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter carrying a volunteer crew from Sumburgh Airport was sent to the scene. Battling fierce winds, the helicopter crew managed to winch all the trawler's crew to safety within a few hours of the grounding. Their bravery earned them awards. The incident, which thankfully had no casualties, prompted the building of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and possibly contributed to the creation of the Search and Rescue helicopter unit currently based at Sumburgh Airport.

Crofting continues to be fundamental to the island's culture. Sheep farming is the dominant agricultural practice, but farmers also raise diverse livestock including cattle, pigs, goats, chickens, ducks, and geese. The pier houses a post office, but no shop exists on the island. Mains electricity arrived relatively late, only in the late 1900s. Visiting yachts can find good shelter in the four main inlets, but strong tides in the Sound of Papa and the northwest region demand careful navigation.

"Angel of Death," the opening track of Slayer's 1986 album *Reign in Blood*, was written by guitarist Jeff Hanneman. The song's lyrics and musical composition are about Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who conducted human experimentation at Auschwitz during World War II. This track has proven controversial for Slayer, resulting in persistent claims that the band harbors Nazi sympathies and racist views.

Even though "Angel of Death" sparked controversy and contributed to the delayed release of Reign in Blood, it has become a signature song for Slayer in concert, featured on every live album and DVD they've produced, and used in numerous movies. The song has garnered critical acclaim, with Steve Huey of AllMusic describing it as a "classic."

Inspired by books he found on tour about Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, Slayer guitarist Jeff Hanneman penned "Angel of Death." Hanneman remembered buying the books, anticipating the disturbing nature of their content. He attributed the song's lyrics to the unsettling details he learned about Mengele from his reading, which stayed with him as the band began creating their album.

The lyrics of the song depict the gruesome surgical experiments conducted by Josef Mengele on prisoners in the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. Mengele's studies centered on groups such as dwarfs and twins, and included both physical and psychological examinations. "Angel of Death" explicitly mentions procedures like live surgeries performed without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, experiments to test the limits of isolation, gassing, deadly germ injections, sex change operations, organ and limb removals, and <unk>.

The lyric "joining heads...rip yourselves apart" references the allegation that Josef Mengele surgically fused twins together, a procedure said to have resulted in severe deformities for one of the children. This claim, detailing how "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back," with "their wrists back to back too," first surfaced during the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann, the "architect of the Holocaust," through the testimony of Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander. Alexander asserted that Mengele "sewed the veins together," essentially creating "Siamese twins." This accusation gained wider notoriety following Alexander's appearance in the 1985 documentary *The Search for Mengele*, a film cited by numerous authors, including Mengele scholar Gerald Posner.

The contentious lyrics of "Angel of Death" contributed to the delayed launch of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Def Jam Records' distributor, Columbia Records, refused to release the album due to the lyrical content and worries about the explicit artwork. Geffen Records eventually released Reign in Blood on October 7, 1986, but the controversy surrounding the album resulted in it being excluded from Geffen Records' official release calendar.
